entries.knowledge: The current diff bundled three changes to the desklamp-plus-non-desklamp skill: (a) a new 'Admissible Actions' section instructing the Actor to verify that a command is present in the current admissible list before issuing it and, when a desired navigation destination is absent but a direct action on that receptacle is listed, to use the direct action instead; (b) a rewrite of the non-desklamp search step to include visible open surfaces such as tables, countertops, shelves, and sidetables, to leave a receptacle that visibly lacks the target, to avoid re-entering a location just left or repeating short cycles, and to prefer an as-yet-untried receptacle type before re-checking a known-empty location; (c) a strengthened exact-category clause stating that near-miss objects must not be acquired, cleaned, cooled, heated, or placed, that a container holding only a non-matching object must be left without manipulating it, and that conditioning or placing a non-target object is not progress. Evidence comes from ten paired tasks (desklamp inspections, ordinary put/clean/transfer tasks, and two tasks whose exact target was absent). Task-level results were identical for Parent and Candidate: each succeeded on 8 and hit the 50-step limit on 2 (the two absent-target tasks), with closely comparable step totals, and the simple desklamp-inspection, put-a-mug, and clean-butterknife pairs were step-for-step identical. The admissible-command instructions did not reliably eliminate inadmissible commands: the Parent emitted an empty action and an unavailable 'go to cabinet 1' (each producing a no-op) and the Candidate emitted an unavailable 'go to cabinet 3' (no-op) shortly before its step limit, and each side then fell back to the listed direct action ('examine' the same cabinet). The only clear step difference was in a clean-soapbar task where the Parent's second action was a malformed output that produced a no-op plus a follow-up empty-inventory check, letting the Candidate finish in 6 steps versus the Parent's 8; this is more plausibly a generation/formatting fallback than an effect of the admissibility clause and rests on a single instance. The expanded-surface search produced occasional new behavior - the Candidate checked an open desk before opening drawers in a put-pencil task and, in the absent-soapbar task, reached receptacle types the Parent never visited (bathtubbasin and a second sinkbasin) - but it still cycled among already-inspected receptacles and did not convert either absent-target task into a success, so the anti-cycling and prefer-new-type wording was not reliably followed. The strengthened no-substitute clause was likewise not reliably followed: in the clean-butterknife task both Parent and Candidate took, cleaned, and moved a knife even though the requested object was a butterknife, while in the clean-soapbar-in-cabinet task both left the visible soapbottle and spraybottle untouched but still failed because no soapbar existed. Because the three components were written together, their individual effects cannot be separated; across these ten pairs the bundle changed neither task-level success nor the dominant cycling/step-limit failure mode, and the observed behavior shifts were marginal and task-specific.

Across several successive edits the exact-category (no-substitute) rule was progressively tightened: near-miss categories were declared non-substitutes; a container holding only a non-matching object was to be left without manipulating that object; and conditioning or placing a non-target was declared non-progress. Adherence is inconsistent. Earlier, when the exact target was absent, the Candidate sometimes abstained while the Parent did not: in a cool-a-pan task the Parent eventually took a pot and cooled and moved it, while the Candidate saw the same pot without taking or moving it; in a heat-a-mug task the Parent took a cup while the Candidate saw the cup and did not manipulate it; and in a later hot-mug task the Parent took cup 2 and heated it while the Candidate left the visible cup untouched and continued searching. In all of those the exact pan or mug was never found and both executions still hit the step limit, so abstention saved only substitution steps and did not create success. The current edit strengthened this clause again inside the rewritten non-desklamp step 2, yet in the current clean-butterknife tasks (requested object 'butterknife', only 'knife' present) both Parent and Candidate took, cleaned, and moved a knife, so the Candidate did not abstain from the near-miss object. Conversely, in the current clean-soapbar-in-cabinet tasks the opened cabinets contained soapbottles and spraybottles and both sides left them unmanipulated, but the exact soapbar was absent and both hit the step limit. The evidence therefore supports only a conditional and unreliable effect: the rule sometimes reduces ineffective near-miss manipulation when the exact target is absent (the Candidate abstained from a pot and a cup in earlier tasks), but it is not consistently followed (a knife was taken for a butterknife), and even when it is followed its task-level value depends on the exact target existing in an inspectable location; these observations do not show the rule improving success by itself, and no observation isolates it from the simultaneous search and admissible-action edits.
